title: {{NAME}} and the Prehistoric Premier League
moral: Every game is better when everyone gets to play.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a muddy-red soccer jersey, dark shorts, and boots caked in prehistoric mud — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The portal opened during regular park training, which meant {{NAME}} was already wearing his boots when a young Triceratops and four confused woodland animals (two badgers, a rabbit, and a fox) arrived in the penalty area.

The Triceratops looked at the football. The football looked back, in the way footballs do.

The Triceratops nudged it with one foot.

It went perfectly into the top corner.

"Hm," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
He organised a match immediately, because the portal clearly wasn't going anywhere and he had a pitch and everyone seemed to be here.

Teams: {{NAME}}, the Triceratops, the fox and one badger versus the other children from training, the rabbit and the second badger.

The Triceratops was, as it turned out, a natural midfielder. The fox was an exceptional striker. The rabbit played defence by sitting directly in front of the goal and refusing to move.

"That's legal," said {{NAME}}, when someone objected.

pages.content:
The match lasted ninety minutes, which is how long the portal stayed open.

Final score was impossible to determine because nobody could agree whether the rabbit counted as a wall or a player when the ball bounced off it and went in.

But the Triceratops scored twice, clean and clear, with a technique that involved its crest: it would crouch slightly to direct the ball with the top of its head.

{{NAME}} spent ten minutes just watching this.

"That's a technique I've never seen before," he said.

The fox tilted its head: obviously.

pages.content:
When the portal began glowing more brightly, {{NAME}} understood it was time.

He walked the Triceratops to the portal edge, the fox and badgers and rabbit following naturally.

The Triceratops turned at the threshold and looked at {{NAME}} with one large eye. Then it made a sound through its crest: a long, resonant note.

"Thank you for the match," said {{NAME}}.

It went through. The fox, badgers, and rabbit followed, having apparently decided the portal was the better option.

The pitch was empty.

"Fair enough," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
He walked home alone, football under his arm, replaying the crest technique.

He tried it in the hallway with a pillow. Unsuccessful.

In bed, he sketched the movement in his notebook: the crouch, the angle, the contact point.

Tomorrow, practice.

He fell asleep with the notebook open, the last page showing the crest technique diagram and one word underneath it: possible.

Somewhere in the past, probably, a Triceratops was doing the same thing.
